en: The Vedāntakārikāvalī composed by Śrī Bucciveṅkaṭācārya.
(Now begins the first chapter, titled "An Exposition of Perception") Having bowed to the lineage of teachers originating from the venerable Rāmādhava,
I compose this *Kārikāvalī*, a collection of verses on the established tenets of Lakṣmaṇa. 1.1.
The category of objects is considered to be twofold by way of the distinction between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
The means of knowledge is threefold, due to the division into perception, inference, and verbal testimony. (1.2)

The object of knowledge is said to be twofold, through the distinction between substance and non-substance. Within this, substance is divided into the insentient and the sentient; here, the insentient is further twofold. (1.3)
Nature, time, and so forth are considered to be twenty-fourfold;
however, time is proclaimed to be threefold according to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). 1.4.
The non-inert [reality], however, is considered to be twofold due to the distinction between the "outward" (parāk) and the "inward" (pratyak).
The outward consists of the eternal manifestation (nityavibhūti) as well as consciousness as an attribute (dharmabhūtajñāna). (1.5)
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva), characterized by the distinction between the inner self and the Lord, is threefold:
bound, liberated, and eternal; the bound soul, moreover, is of two kinds. (1.6)

Furthermore, those who desire enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*), and those who desire both (*bubhukṣu*) are each divided into two types, based on the distinction between being intent upon wealth and pleasure (*arthakāmapara*) or intent upon dharma (*dharmapara*). (1.7)
One who is devoted to another deity, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, and one who is devoted to Dharma—these are three types.
Furthermore, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) is considered to be of two kinds, based on the attainment of isolation (kaivalya) or final liberation (mokṣa). || 1.8 ||

He, however, who is intent on liberation is of two kinds, distinguished as the devotee (*bhakta*) and the one who has sought refuge (*prapanna*). The one who has sought refuge is further divided into two types: the single-minded (*ekāntin*) and the supremely single-minded (*paramaikāntin*). (1.9)
The Supreme One, who is the sole object of devotion, is described as being twofold—as the Proud and the Afflicted;
and the Lord is divided fivefold according to the distinctions of the Para, Vyūha, and other forms. (1.10)
Furthermore, the single [Vāsudeva] manifests as a fourfold array through the divisions of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. 1.11.
The Fish and other incarnations are proclaimed to be infinite in number;
however, the Lord as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) resides within every body.
The *arcāvatāra* (incarnation in the form of an image) resides in places such as Śrīraṅga and Veṅkaṭādri;
however, Keśava and others are described by the knowers of reality as a different manifestation (*vyūha*). (1.13)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction, and power—these are considered the ten kinds of non-substance (adravya). 1.14.

The instrument for that valid cognition is proclaimed to be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Valid cognition is that which conforms to the practical usage of a single object as it truly exists. (1.15)
It is not the case that doubt, false knowledge, and erroneous cognition are the same;
for doubt is a cognition whose object consists of multiple things regarding a single substratum. (1.16)
Intellect (dhī), when there is a perversion regarding the property (dharma), is declared to be knowledge otherwise;
that same intellect, when there is a perversion regarding the substratum (dharmin), is considered a perverted cognition.
Perception is declared to be the means of valid cognition that causes direct realization;
this direct realization is of two kinds: conceptual and non-conceptual. (1.18)
The apprehension of the first lump is called non-conceptual; the apprehension of the second lump would be conceptual cognition. (1.19)
This [perception] is seen to be both dependent on the sense faculties and independent of them.
The independent is considered to be of two kinds: that which is established by itself and that which is divine. (1.20)
That which is born of yoga is self-established, whereas the other is born from the favor of a master;
the wise declare that all of this [latter] is merely recent. (1.21)
The knowledge of the eternally liberated Lord is said to be beginningless;
for memory is indeed a valid means of cognition that arises from a prior experience. (1.22)

When the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened by means such as perception of a similar object or reflection, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), like memory, is included within the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (1.23)
Even the perfection of a meritorious person is considered here to be intuitive insight (*pratibhā*);
"all knowledge is according to reality"—this is the statement of Yamuna. (1.24)
The absence of a jar on the ground is indeed the very nature of the ground itself, and nothing else;
the prior absence of a clay jar is [the clay], and its destruction is the potsherd. (1.25)

For it is the unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) that is denoted by the word "difference" (bheda). In some cases, the cognition of a counter-correlative (pratiyogitva) is produced by the very nature of the word itself. (1.26)
The consciousness of the internal organ, through its modification and by means of the object, attains identity with consciousness and thus produced direct realization. || 1.27 ||
All such statements as these, propounded by others, are not accepted here;
neither generality (sāmānya), nor inherence (samavāya), nor particularity (viśeṣa) is accepted here. (1.28)
The postulation of a distinction between qualities within the category of qualities such as number and the rest—which contradicts the author of the Sūtras—will all be refuted. (1.29)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Definition of Perception," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Inference") Inference is considered the instrument for the self-cognition that is inferential knowledge (*anumiti*).
That [inference] consists of the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), while its cause is held to be the cognition of pervasion (*vyāptidhī*). (2.1)

Pervasion (vyāpti) is said to be the state of not occurring in the locus of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvādhikaraṇāvṛttitvam). The cognition of this pervaded [reason] as residing in the subject (pakṣavṛttitva) receives the name "subsumptive reflection" (parāmarśa). (2.2)
The cognition of the probandum in the subject arising therefrom is considered to be of the nature of inference.
Through a single cognition characterized by a preponderance of concomitance, the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti) arises. (2.3)
The similar instance (sapakṣa) is that which possesses the probandum as previously ascertained;
the subject (pakṣa) is that in which the probandum is suspected; and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is that which lacks it. (2.4)
The reason (hetu) is of two types: positive (anvayin) and negative (vyatirekin).

Furthermore, [the fallacious reasons are] the deviant (vyabhicārin), the contradictory (viruddha), the unestablished (asiddha), and that which has a counter-balancing argument (satpratipakṣaka). || 2.5 ||
And "sublated" (bādhita)—these five are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) that are not proof-givers. Thus has the detailed exposition of inference for oneself (svārthānumāna) been described. (2.6)
The reflection (*parāmarśa*) produced by the *nyāya* serves for the sake of inference for others (*parārthānumiti*).
The *nyāya* consists of the five-membered sentences, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*). (2.7)

The thesis is the statement of that which is to be proven; the reason is considered to be the statement of that [thesis]. The example would be the speech of an instance preceded by the statement of pervasion. (2.8)
The application (upanaya) is considered to be the cognition that the pervaded [reason] resides in the subject;
furthermore, the statement of conclusion (nigamana) is the restatement [of the thesis]. (2.9)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Inference," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.

(Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Verbal Testimony") A statement uttered by one who is not untrustworthy is traditionally held to be the instrument of verbal knowledge (*śabda*). Since the Veda is not of human origin, this definition applies to it as well. (3.1)
Since linguistic proficiency exists regarding established entities, the Veda conveys perfected knowledge;
therefore, its lack of authority should not be suspected on the grounds that it would forfeit its status as being intent upon [established] effects. (3.2)
Because it designates both karma and Brahman, it consists of two parts:
the first part is devoted to karma, while the latter pertains to the sphere of Brahman. (3.3)
Because of the identity of the preceding and succeeding [sections], they should indeed be explained as a single treatise;
for even when there is a division into chapters, the unity of the treatise is not contradicted. (3.4)
It is understood to be threefold, consisting of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), and mantras.
A mantra is that which makes known the matter to be performed; the speech of an arthavāda is [that which provides praise]. (3.5)
That which incites activity is an injunction; the sentence that prompts action is the injunctive statement.
It is threefold, distinguished as apūrva, niyama, and parisaṅkhyā. (3.6)
They are considered to be of many kinds—namely, the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya).
Their essential natures and defining characteristics are to be understood according to other systems of logic.
Prosody, ritual, phonetics, etymology, astronomy, and grammar—these are declared to be the six ancillary limbs (aṅga) of the Veda. (3.8)

The *Chandas* [Veda] consists of the *anuṣṭubh* and other meters; the *Kalpa* provides instruction on the *śrauta* and other rituals; the *Śikṣā* determines the phonemes; and the *Nirukta* explains the meaning of words. (3.9)
For determining the time for performance and so forth, astronomy is authoritative;
for the correctness of words, grammar is authoritative—thus there is authority in all the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas). 3.10.
The authority of the Smṛtis and other texts is declared on the basis of this [Veda];
whatever is contrary to this cannot attain the status of valid knowledge. (3.11)

This [set of conditions], beginning with expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) and so forth, is the sole cause of verbal cognition; its investigation has been summarized here by me, fearing excessive prolixity in this work. (3.12)
That word is considered to be of two kinds, by way of being primary or figurative.
Denotation (abhidhā) is the primary function, while any other function is figurative (aupacārikī). (3.13)
Words that denote the body function by referring to the embodied being;
it shall be declared that Hari is the single denotable object of all words. (3.14)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Verbal Testimony," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(The determination of the means of valid cognition is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature [of Objects]":
That which is the object of a valid cognition is the "object of cognition" (*prameya*); thus, it is of two kinds.
That which is "substance" (dravya), "non-substance" (adravya), and so forth, is its material cause (upādānakāraṇa). || 4.1 ||
Being the locus of different states is called "substantial causality" (upādānatva);
or, substance may be that which is the substratum of qualities, and that is proclaimed to be of two kinds. (4.2)
The absence of mixed *sattva* is designated as "insentience" (*jaḍatva*). Both *prakṛti* and *kāla* are insentient; that [absence] consists of the three qualities, beginning with *sattva*. (4.3)

That *prakṛti* is designated by the terms "the perishable," "ignorance" (*avidyā*), and "illusion" (*māyā*). It is called "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*) because it exists in a state oriented toward its effects. (4.4)
From the unmanifest arises the Great Principle (mahat) through the distinctions of being characterized by sattva and so forth;
from that arises the ego (ahaṅkāra), which likewise possesses the threefold distinction of being characterized by sattva and so forth.
"By way of its divisions, there are indeed other names for those who possess the nature of the ego—namely, the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*. (4.6)
From among those, from the modified *ahaṃkāra*—the *sāttvika* ego-sense when refined—the eleven organs arise, consisting of the nature of both the organs of cognition and the organs of action. (4.7)
That which is capable of the expansion of knowledge is called the organ of knowledge; it is considered to consist of the mind, the ear, the eye, the skin, the nose, and the tongue. (4.8)
The mind is the cause of memory and so forth, and the cause of bondage, liberation, and the like;
that which has the capacity to grasp mere sound is called the sense-organ of hearing. (4.9)
The eye grasps only form; the skin is the cause for grasping touch; the nose grasps only odor; and the tongue illuminates taste. (4.10)
The connection of these [organs] with their objects is proclaimed to be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
The organs of action are considered to possess a single capacity for actions such as articulation. (4.11)
It is fivefold, distinguished as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Speech is the cause for the utterance of phonemes; the hand is the instrument for crafts and the like. (4.12)
The foot is for the purpose of movement; the anus effects the evacuation of waste; the generative organ is considered the cause of supreme bliss for both women and men. (4.13)
Furthermore, from the tamasic ego, conjoined with rajasic egoity,
there arises the subtle element of sound and the rest, which is the cause of the gross elements.

They say that the subtle element (*tanmātra*) is a substance consisting of a specific prior state of extreme subtlety belonging to the very elements; it is fivefold, corresponding to the five elements. (4.15)

The pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra) is recognized as the substratum for sound and the other [objects]; among them, the subtle element of sound is the primary material cause of the gross elements. (4.16)

From the subtle element of touch arise the subtle elements of form and taste; from these [along with the subtle element of smell] arises the subtle element of odor. From these [five subtle elements] arise ether, air, fire, water, and earth. (4.17)
The five gross elements are now described as having the nature of the subtle elements (tanmātra);
they represent the intermediate state between the tamasic ego and the primordial pair [of intellect and ego], occurring at the beginning of the yuga.
From this [tanmātra], the subtle element of sound, space likewise arises;
it is space itself that is designated as "direction" through the movement of the sun. (4.19)
That substance, when perfectly joined with the intermediate state between space and air, is the subtle element of touch; and from this, air is produced in due order.
The substance of air and fire, conjoined with their intermediate state, is called the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra); from this, fire is produced in due order.
The substance consisting of fire and water, joined with the intermediate state, is called the subtle element of taste; from this, indeed, water is born. (4.22)
The substance consisting of water and earth, joined with the intermediate state, is called the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra); from this, that earth arises. (4.23)
The first is said to possess sound; the second possesses both sound and touch; the third possesses form, sound, and touch; and so too does the fourth. (4.24)

The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are said to be joined with form, sound, touch, and taste, with smell as the additional [quality]; and from these, the five gross elements (bhūtas) likewise arise. || 4.25 ||
Thus, the distinction between the twenty-four principles—beginning with Prakṛti, Avyakta, Mahat, and so forth—has been well-determined and established in their proper sequence. (4.26)
Having created the elements, the Blessed One divided each one into two; having made each one twofold, he then divided another into four parts. (4.27)
Having divided those portions into four parts, he joined them together in their respective portions;
with his own portions augmented by a fourth part each, he brought forth the five elements.
Even though other elemental components were present, the designation "earth," "water," "fire," "air," and "space" arose in the world because of the predominance of their own respective parts. (4.29)

The Śruti indicates that this quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) is to be understood as an embellishment of the septuplication (saptīkṛti) of the elements, along with the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego (ahaṅkāra). (4.30)
The five elements, the unmanifest, the great principle (mahat), and the ego (ahaṅkāra)—these are the material causes of the body and the sense organs for each individual soul. 4.31.
Indeed, various ornaments that last for an eon adorn the body; yet that which is governed solely by consciousness is what is truly called the "body. (4.32)
The body is of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal; O Blessed One, that which belongs to the eternal sūris is indeed eternal and innate. (4.33)
That [universe], though impermanent, is also twofold according to whether it is produced by karma or not produced by karma;
that which is not produced by karma is fashioned by the will of the Lord and others. (4.34)
And that [attainment] produced by karma is twofold: that which is accompanied by one's own will, and that which is produced by karma alone;
as in the case of Saubhari and others, it is the former.
The second [category] belongs to those such as ourselves and is generally twofold:
stationary and mobile. Among these, that which consists of stone and the like is considered stationary. (4.36)
The mobile [world] is said to be of two kinds: born from a womb and not born from a womb. That which is born from a womb consists of the divisions of gods, humans, animals, and so forth. (4.37)

The womb-born, the sweat-born, the egg-born, the hellish, and that which is not born from a womb—thus it is taught that the fivefold elements (pañcīkṛta) possess the power to produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). 4.38.

Creation prior to the emergence of the cosmic egg is the collective creation (samaṣṭi), while that which follows is the individual creation (vyaṣṭi); thus, according to the Vedāntins, creation is twofold. (4.39)
The state of "greatness" (mahattva) and so forth is held to be a different condition of the unmanifest (avyakta) and the rest;
if a state that is of a different genus were considered a different principle (tattvāntara), [then this would follow]. (4.40)

Thus, through the categories known as the unmanifest (avyakta), mahat, ego (ahaṅkāra), and the senses, the principles (tattvas) become twenty-fourfold, including the subtle elements (tanmātras). (4.41)

The objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment arise, as appropriate, for the Lord and for the individual soul from primordial nature (prakṛti) and the other categories. 4.42.

The object of experience consists of the eyes and so forth; the instruments of experience are considered to be [the sense organs]; the place of experience is the world-realm (bhuvana), for it contains those born from eggs and the like. (4.43)
Thus, that which is commenced by the fivefold elements (pañcīkṛtabhūta) is the primordial matter (prākṛta); it is called the "egg" (aṇḍa), shaped like a wood-apple fruit (kapitthaphala). || 4.44 ||
This entire Jambūdvīpa is surrounded by the salt ocean;
beyond that, Plakṣadvīpa is encircled by the Ikṣu ocean.
Beyond that is Śālmalidvīpa, surrounded by the ocean of wine;
and beyond that is Kuśadvīpa, encompassed by the ocean of clarified butter.
After that, Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded by the ocean of curd;
after that, Śākadvīpa is encircled by the ocean of milk.
All this, surrounding Puṣkaradvīpa, is encircled by a pure ocean;
beyond that is a ring-mountain consisting of golden ground.
He too is enveloped in darkness, and he too by the waters of the womb;
from that, there arises a single cosmic egg, both above and below the earth.
There may be such infinite eggs of the Great Hari, resembling bubbles upon the water, as described in succession in the Purāṇas. (4.50)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Primordial Nature," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(Now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Time") That which is devoid of the three qualities is called inert time (*kāla*).
That time is considered to be of two kinds, through the distinction between the indivisible and the divisible. 5.1
The first is the all-pervading [time], which causes the cognition of past, future, and present;
it is considered to have many divisions according to distinctions such as the blink of an eye and so forth. (5.2)
This time is understood to be eternal precisely because it is indivisible;
however, with respect to its own effects, time serves as the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa). 5.3
Therefore, let it be understood that he is not eternal in his form as an effect;
in the realm of his playful manifestation (līlāvibhūti), the Lord performs actions by depending upon time.
But this [time] does not depend upon time within the eternal manifestation (nityavibhūti); rather, this time is merely an accessory for the sport (krīḍā) of the Supreme Self. 5.5
The constant, occasional, and primordial dissolutions are caused by time;
thus has the description of the true nature of time been elucidated. (5.6)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Time," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.

(Now begins the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Eternal Glory") Non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) is the characteristic found in pure being (*śuddhasattva*), in objective knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), in the individual soul (*jīva*), and in the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, that [non-inertness] consists in self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*).

The characteristic of the first two [categories] is held to be insentience (ajaḍatā) while being external (parāktve sati). Being manifest to another is what is designated as "externality" (parāktvam). (6.2)
The region consisting solely of pure sattva is insentient; it is limited in the lower region and infinite in the upward direction. (6.3)
This self-luminous form, consisting of the five Upaniṣads, is the eternal manifestation of Viṣṇu, eternally composed of bliss. (6.4)
This manifestation of the Lord is considered to consist of objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment, even for those whose selves are eternally liberated.
The first object of enjoyment is the body of the Lord and so forth; the second is sandalwood and the like;
while the place of enjoyment is said to be the ruby-arched gateways and such. (6.6)
The bodies of the eternal lords are fashioned by the eternal will of Hari;
however, the bodies and so forth of the liberated are considered to be produced by their own resolve.
For Lord Hari, who exists as the manifestation, the expansion, the image, and the incarnation of the Lord of Śrī, his non-material bodies [are established] immediately following the consecration.
For when [the Lord] becomes inclined toward grace, [His powers] indeed become manifest;
and that manifestation of His is said to be dependent upon His will. (6.9)
As for the question of how there can be contact between a natural and a non-natural body, that is sufficient;
for such a thing is frequently observed in the incarnations of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.
But know those qualities such as brilliance and so forth in Hari’s divine and auspicious form through the investigation of the *Gadyatraya*. (6.11)
As for the statement that is seen regarding the bodilessness of the liberated, that refers to the absence of connection with a body produced by karma. (6.12)
The primordial Vedānta teachers describe the divine and auspicious form of Śrīnātha according to this sequence mentioned in the Purāṇas.
This great manifestation of the Lord, designated by such terms as Tripādvibhūti, Vaikuṇṭha, and Paravyoma, is most highly glorified.
In this [city], there flourishes a city named Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with twelve enclosures and possessing many hundreds of gate-towers.
There, a celestial abode named Ānanda is clearly manifest;
there, an assembly hall shines, featuring a thousand pillars made of jewels.
And there, Ananta shone, resplendent with the luster of the jewels upon his hoods;
upon him was situated the lion-throne accompanied by Dharma and the other [virtues].
There, an eight-petalled lotus shines, worshipped by Vimala and others with chowries in their hands; therein resides Śeṣa, whose nature is consciousness.
Therein, the one consisting of bliss, directly beyond the reach of all words,
shines in the form of wondrous light as the self of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eternal Manifestation," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.

(Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Knowledge as an Attribute") Just as light is an attribute of a lamp or of the self, so too is that consciousness which exists as an attribute; it is eternal in the case of the eternal Lords. (7.1)
In bound souls it is concealed; in liberated souls it was previously hidden.
Through contraction and expansion, it undergoes destruction, origination, and maturation. (7.2)
If knowledge is contracted through the doors of the senses, it undergoes contraction;
if there is expansion through the doors of the senses, it results from the spreading forth of knowledge. (7.3)
It is agreed that this [consciousness] is self-luminous and is a means of valid cognition by itself;
its self-luminosity is like that of a lamp, insofar as it brings about its own manifestation as well as that of others. (7.4)
Due to the proximity of a particular state of darkness, knowledge is concealed during sleep;
its substantiality as well as its quality of luminosity [is obscured].
The various types of cognition—pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—are not distinct from it [the self].
The statements "I hate" and "I desire," however, are considered to be like "I remember" and so forth. (7.6)
Memory and the other faculties are infinite varieties of knowledge functioning within the individual soul;
likewise, the attributes of the Blessed Lord are infinite expansions of both knowledge and power.
This meaning has been proclaimed by the Great Teacher in the *Gadyatraya*;
it is understood through the commentary on those respective essential natures. (7.8)
The Lord, being well-pleased by devotion and surrender, is the bestower of liberation;
therefore, devotion and surrender are indeed the supreme cause of liberation. (7.9)
They have declared that the yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge are the means for devotion;
[the former is] action performed as worship of the Lord, free from any desire for results.
Contemplation within a purified inner organ constitutes the yoga of knowledge;
whether directly or otherwise, both of these serve as causes for devotion.
The yoga of devotion consists of eight limbs; it is an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness, produced through discernment and other means, which has attained the form of direct perception.

At the time of the conclusion of each respective body, this very instrumental devotion (sādhanabhakti), which is subject to transformation, is considered to be accompanied by the limb of surrender (prapatti). 7.13.
But the enjoyment of the fruit arises from the grace of the Blessed One;
for this very reason, Hari directly attains the state of being the perfected means.
Due to the distinctions between the Antarāditya-vidyā and others, that [knowledge] is considered manifold;
yet all of this is the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), which serves as the means for attaining Brahman.
The science of Nyāsa is surrender (prapatti), which possesses five limbs:
the resolve for favorability and the avoidance of unfavorability; || 7.16 ||
The five limbs are said to be: confidence that [the Lord] will protect, the choice of Him as protector, and the state of helplessness in surrendering oneself. (7.17)
This [knowledge] is to be understood by the wise as arising from approaching a guru;
it is said to effect the destruction of the attachment to past and future sins. (7.18)
"Without any transgression, there is no other who acts as an obstacle for those who know Brahman; thus is the teaching of the Great Teacher to be understood. (7.19)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Knowledge as an Attribute," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Living Being") Consciousness residing in an atom is stated to be the defining characteristic of the living being (*jīva*).
And that [living being] is held to be distinct from the body, the sense organs, and so forth. (8.1)

The experience of manifold objects by the individual soul (jīva), though it is atomic in size, is clearly evident; for that, the pervasion of its attribute-like consciousness (dharmabhūtavijñāna) is necessary. 8.2
Because of its connection with the recollection of objects previously experienced, it is eternal; yet it is distinct in each body, as indicated by such terms as "the enjoyer" and so forth. (8.3)
In relation to primordial nature (prakṛti), the embodied soul is the body; in relation to the glorious [Self], its self-luminosity is taught by direct perception and the Vedas. 8.4
They have declared that even for an atom, the perception of results such as [movement to] another location arises from a consciousness called *adṛṣṭa*, which is produced by karma. (8.5)
The individual soul (jīva) is considered to be of three kinds: bound, liberated, and eternal.
From Brahmā down to the smallest insect, those who are joined to the cycle of worldly existence are the bound. (8.6)

Those who are proficient in the aims of the three-fold group [of dharma, artha, and kāma] and who desire worldly enjoyment are described as being intent on wealth and pleasure, identifying their self solely with their own bodies. (8.7)
But those people there were devoted to dharma, being intent upon the performance of sacrifices and other such rites;
for dharma is the means of attaining supramundane welfare, as declared by the Vedic injunction (codanā). (8.8)
Those devoted to the worship of Rudra and others are considered to be intent on other deities;
those who are afflicted, those seeking knowledge, and those seeking wealth—thus are the Bhāgavatas remembered. (8.9)
And the characteristic of those seeking liberation who are intent upon absolute isolation is stated:
it is the supreme experience of one's own self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti). (8.10)
Even after attaining the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) and reaching the supreme station by way of the path of light,
one remains in some corner like a woman abandoned by her lover.
This state of absolute isolation (kaivalya) is accepted only by some noble ones; however, it is established that our noble ones do not accept such isolation. 8.12

Devotees, through the very devotion previously described, are those who desire the attainment of liberation; in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, it is clear that Śūdras lack the qualification for such devotion.
Devotees are considered to be of two kinds, according to their devotion to the goal (sādhya) or to the means (sādhana).
Those such as Parāṅkuśa and others are known as the former, while those such as Vyāsa and others are known as the latter.
Those seeking liberation and those who have surrendered are practitioners of yoga characterized by poverty and other such qualities;
they are further divided into two types: those devoted to the three aims of life and those devoted to liberation.
Those who pursued virtue, wealth, and pleasure for the sake of their master were the first;
through association with the virtuous, they became devoted to detachment from worldly objects and to the desire for liberation. (8.16)

Others, having taken refuge in a great teacher for the sake of attaining the enjoyments of the Blessed One, rely solely on *prapatti* (surrender) due to their incapacity in [the practice of] devotion and the like. 8.17.
The wise have declared that surrender possesses universal authority;
those who are single-mindedly devoted desire its fruit to be everything other than liberation.
Those who are supremely single-minded desire only the pleasure of the Blessed One;
he who desires liberation only after having experienced the fruits of his commenced karma. (8.19)
Arrogant yet afflicted in this cycle of existence, as if being scorched in a fire, he who desires liberation at the very moment immediately following his surrender; (8.20)

Through association with the virtuous, the person who possesses the path described in the two excellent verses has his own true nature manifested; he is liberated and partakes in the experience of Brahman.
Regarding the mere experience of enjoyment by the liberated one, equality is enjoined in the Śrutis;
his wandering through all worlds according to his own will is not obstructed. (8.22)
And for one who is liberated, the freedom of will is obtained as dependent upon the resolve of Hari;
however, the scripture concerning non-return serves to prohibit the recurrence of karma.
Ananta, Garuḍa, and others are eternal, possessing ever-uncontracted knowledge; by the eternal command of the Lord, they are eternally devoted to His service. (8.24)
The descent and other manifestations of these [sages] occur solely by their own will, like that of Hari; yet their status as authorized agents was ordained by the Lord.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Definition of the Individual Soul," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Definition of God") The defining characteristic of God is indeed being the sovereign over all others except Himself;
He is the subtle cause of the universe, consisting of the mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness. 9.1
This very [Lord], endowed with volition (saṅkalpa), is considered the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa);
and by virtue of being the inner controller (antaryāmin) of time and so forth, He is also the auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa). || 9.2 ||
In its form as the effect, it is called the manifold material cause; by virtue of being the transformer, it is also considered the efficient cause. (9.3)
And that would be a cooperative cause by virtue of assisting in the production of the effect, according to the doctrine that all cognitions are accompanied by a single cognition. (9.4)
The very nature of being the material cause (upādānatva) has been stated in the case of the Lord, just as it is in the case of clay and so forth;
His causality as the efficient cause (nimittatva), like that of a potter, is due to His volition expressed in the words, "He thought" (tadaikṣata).
Its state of being a cooperative cause is also declared in the Antaryāmi-Brāhmaṇa;
words such as "Being," "Brahman," and "Self" convey its nature as the cause. (9.6)

In that regard, according to the maxim of the goat-sacrifice, those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa are considered [to be the true sacrificers]; for [the state] is endowed with a condition that is unfit for the differentiation of name and form. (9.7)
The one whose nature is Brahman is held to be joined with the extremely subtle consciousness and unconsciousness;
indeed, no differentiation is perceived prior to the division into name and form. (9.8)
Therefore, even in the case of a clay pot and the like, that [clay] is said to be one;
and due to the absence of name, form, and so forth, it is also designated by the word "Being" (sat).

That very [Brahman], by entering within, effects the differentiation of name and form, just as the individual soul (jīva), having entered within, partakes in the differentiation of name and form. 9.10
And by words such as "I am a god," [the self] is denoted in its primary sense, just as words like "blue" denote that which is invariably associated with blue and so forth. (9.11)
They declare that the primary meaning alone is distinguished and free from limiting conditions;
likewise, the Blessed One is the inner controller of both name and form.
The one who performs the division is denoted by those words in their primary sense; the claim made by others that these words have a non-primary meaning is not logical. 9.13.
Because they are not distinct from the body and so forth, words other than those used for extraction will, in reality, denote only that which is qualified and possessed of excellence. (9.14)
For this very reason, expressions such as "All is Brahman" and "This has that as its self" are joined through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya). || 9.15 ||
In our view, the scriptural texts concerning difference are established on the basis of the difference between essential natures;
likewise, the scriptural texts concerning non-difference are also easily reconciled through the non-difference of the qualified entity. (9.16)

The effect is not something other than this gross [world] produced from the subtle cause composed of consciousness and unconsciousness; this is clearly established in the *ārambhaṇa-adhikaraṇa* and other sections. 9.17.
There are certain scriptural passages devoted to the qualitylessness [of Brahman]; these certainly teach its freedom from those qualities that are to be abandoned. (9.18)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of God," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Non-Substances") Having thus determined substance (*dravya*), non-substance (*adravya*) is now determined.
Sattva is considered to be of two kinds: pure sattva and mixed sattva. (10.1)
That which is untouched by rajas and tamas is called pure sattva; however, that which is mixed with rajas and tamas is proclaimed as mixed sattva.
That which is beyond the senses and is the cause of illumination and so forth is designated as *sattva*;
*rajas* is proclaimed to be the cause of greed, activity, and so forth; and [the cause of] *tamas* is [as follows]. (10.3)
The three qualities (guṇas) have negligence, delusion, and so forth as their causes; they are equal during dissolution, but become unbalanced during emergence and the other stages. 10.4

Sound is the quality perceived by the ear; it is twofold, consisting of articulated letters and non-articulated sounds. Arising from the palate, a drum, and so forth, it resides within the five elements.

Tangibility is that which is apprehended by the tactile faculty; it exists in the four [elements] beginning with earth, while its specific divisions such as cold, heat, and so forth, have been described in other treatises. (10.6)
This form, which is apprehended by the faculty of the eye, is of four kinds; it is first divided into two types based on the distinctions of white, red, yellow, and black. (10.7)
By virtue of being luminous or non-luminous, that which is luminous resides in fire;
this same [element] is declared to be non-luminous in earth and water. (10.8)
Taste, which is apprehended by the sense of the tongue, is proclaimed to be of six kinds;
smell, the quality apprehended by the nose, is of two kinds, as found in other treatises. (10.9)
Odor belongs to earth alone; taste belongs to earth and water;
form belongs to earth, water, and fire; and touch belongs to these three together with air.
Sound is said to predominate in the five elements;
however, according to the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), all [elements] are present everywhere.
In the context of the associated condition (*saṃyukta-pratyaya*), the cause is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
That conjunction is considered to be of two kinds, distinguished by whether it pertains to an effect or a non-effect. (10.12)
The conjunction of all-pervading substances, such as ether and the hand, is considered both possible and impossible;
however, the conjunction of two all-pervading substances is held to be impossible by both scripture and reasoning. (10.13)
Therefore, the conjunction of time with the Lord is also well-accepted;
for disjunction, being of the nature of the absence of conjunction, is not a separate quality.
In all causes, it is accepted that there exists a power which carries out the state of being a cause;
this [power] is well-known in the case of gems, mantras, and so forth, yet it is beyond the reach of the senses.
The eight beginning with intellect (buddhi) enter into consciousness (vijñāna), as do the latent impression (bhāvanā) and those occurring in the interval:
fluidity (dravatva), viscidity (sneha), number (saṅkhyāna), dimension (parimāṇa), and momentum (vega). || 10.16 ||
Because it consists of the very nature of the substance itself, it does not exceed [the category of substance];
therefore, *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) is included within this [category of] conjunction. 10.17.
Since separateness consists in the absence of conjunction, like disjunction, and since gravity is also a power, there is no additional category anywhere. (10.18)
Some wise men say that even karmas possess the nature of power (śakti), while others who know the Vedānta declare them to be distinct entities (padārthāntara). 10.19.
Following the path of the ancient texts, this refutation of the doctrine of Viśiṣṭādvaita has been presented here according to my understanding. (10.20)
The *Kārikāvalī* was composed by Śrīmad Veṅkaṭadāsa, the third son of the venerable Āryādhvarīndra. 10.21.
This series of verses has been composed by me, desiring to instill joy in one whose supreme and most wonderful splendor is dependent upon Ramā. 10.22.

I offer this series of verses on our own philosophical system, enriched by the enumeration of the number of fingers [on the hands], unto the two lotus-feet of the Lotus-navelled Lord (Viṣṇu), which are like the presiding deities of devotion and surrender. 10.23.

The illustrious Aṇṇārya, who was like a moon arisen from the ocean of the lineage of the venerable Śrīmat-Śaṭhamarṣaṇa, adorned the four systems of philosophy with the splendor of his words; his son, the wise Śrī-Veṅkaṭārya, who has mastered the principles of right conduct, has composed this *Kārikā* on the lineage of the Upaniṣads for the great delight of the virtuous.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Non-Substances," in the Vedāntakārikāvalī.
(The determination of the objects of knowledge is completed.
Thus ends the *Vedāntakārikāvalī* composed by the venerable Bucciveṅkaṭācārya.
